column1: Directed by Livi Kessel. 55 minutes (followed by Survivor-Speaks discussion). Not Rated. In Hebrew with English

This screening will be followed by a panel discussion with domestic abuse survivors, coordinated by Finding Our Voices. Finding Our Voices is the grassroots nonprofit breaking the silence of domestic abuse around Maine, including in schools, and providing practical resources and heart-healing support to women survivors and their
Registration for this screening is recommended, and admission is pay-what-you-want.

When teenage Livi is the first in her friend group to move in with a man, her girl friends are excited for her. But her world slowly gets smaller and more dangerous as he increasingly isolates and psychologically terrorizes

The powerful documentary chronicles Livi’s journey against Prof. Jane Monkton Smith’s chilling and seminal timeline of the eight stages that precede intimate partner murder. Through Livi’s conversations with those who knew her while she was trapped in the domestic abuse, the film illuminates the dangerous gray zone of psychological abuse AKA coercive control that often hides in plain

Topics of the post-screening discussion will include how to best help someone you worry is trapped in an unhealthy intimate partner relationship, and the role the community can play in safeguarding our neighbors from dangerous family
For more information about Finding Our Voices visit https://findingourvoices.net

column1: Directed by Jack Auen and Kevin Walker. 100 minutes. Not Rated. In French, English, German, and Italian with English

column1: Directed by Adam Khalil and Zack Khalil. 80 minutes. Not Rated. In English and Anishinaabemowin with English

Aanikoobijigan [ancestor / great-grandparent / great-grandchild] documents the emotional and vital work of MACPRA (Michigan Anishinaabek Cultural Preservation and Repatriation Alliance). This alliance, made up of repatriation specialists representing all Michigan tribes, fights to bring their Ancestors and funerary objects home from settler colonial institutions like museums, libraries, and

Adam and Zack Khalil’s monumental and formally daring film follows the pressing struggle to rebury Indigenous human remains that have been held in sterile storage, laying bare the history of Indigenous collections and the battle to recognize and enforce the laws intended to facilitate their repatriation to the communities they were originally stolen from. Using an essayistic approach alongside vérité portraits, the film celebrates the courageous individuals who carry out this hard and emotionally draining labor of return. — Sundance Film

Burt Lancaster stars as Ned Merrill, a man who confronts his destiny by swimming home, pool by pool, through the suburban nightmare of upper-class East Coast society. This screening will be followed by a discussion with director Ian

If you were invited to sit at a table with someone you’ve never met before and answer handwritten questions from a wooden box about the state of America, would you run the other way? The Work in Progress invites strangers from across generations and geographies to engage in candid discussions about America’s ever-evolving democracy, identity, and definitions of community — and where the heck we go from here. Guided by questions posed by Executive Producer Robert Reich, participants sit down in a series of conversations with one another to explore the country they’re living in now and the one they still believe is

These encounters are intercut with portraits of Americans at work — in woodshops, laboratories, fields, board rooms, recording studios, theaters, and beyond. The message is simple but profound: America can work because, in many ways, it’s already working. And a central part of the work ahead is to reclaim the practices of dialogue, debate, compromise, and perhaps most importantly, listening, so that we might find our footing

With their uncle (Michael Redgrave) completely disinterested in his wards, Giddens witnesses a series of unsettling events that leads her to believe that their house is haunted, and the children possessed. column1: Sascha Braunig (b. 1983, Qualicum Beach, BC) devotes her critical focus to the capaciousness and limitations of the feminine form under duress. Braunig’s figures teeter towards overextension—waists are pinched to extremity
column2: appendages are restricted or decked in barbs
column3: phantom silhouettes sinuously negotiate and adapt to the contours of their technicolor environments. Drawing on feminist artistic discourse, Braunig’s imaginaries engage the ways that gender performance and systems of power are replicated. Training, fitting, and reinforcement are recurring motifs in the severe and sometimes sinister crucibles which Braunig’s figures endure. Cast in vibrant complementary palettes and anchored through Braunig’s graphic, tensile formal vocabulary, her images recapitulate and usurp foundational codes of gendered visuality to create surreal and unequivocally emblematic&nbsp
